description:
Team & Core Competencies

We are a multidisciplinary engineering team with proven experience in optimization modeling, data science, software architecture, and modern web applications. Our track record includes successfully delivering end-to-end projects involving orbital mechanics analytics, space trajectory data, algorithmic decision-making, and interactive high-performance dashboards. We operate as an integrated, agile, and pre-established unit.
summary:
Lunar Landing Navigator is a browser-running mission simulation that shows how much power a landing point in the 9 possible candidate regions on the Lunar south pole of Artemis III will receive and when it will be able to communicate directly with Earth.

At the pole, the Sun and the Earth travel only a few degrees above the horizon, so the actual land horizon determines the result. We calculate the horizon from NASA LOLA altitude data, the positions of the Sun and the Earth hour by hour with NASA/JPL SPICE. The user selects a region, lands on the terrain and plays the year. He sees live how the shadows sweep the terrain, the Earth oscillates on the horizon, whether the battery withstands long darkness and how the antenna share changes communication.

This difference is important: an account that counts the horizon as flat finds 50% sunny time in Malapert, while the result with the real terrain turns out to be 65%. The wrong horizon means the wrong landing point and the wrong battery selection. We are producing the scene that NASA shows in a single video live for every region and every date. The figures are a preliminary result; verification with the NASA enlightenment map has continued.
details:
What exactly does it do?

!0aSS is a mission simulator that runs in a web browser. For each of the 9 Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole, it shows how much sunlight a landing site receives and when it can communicate directly with Earth. Users choose a region on a polar map, watch a short landing sequence, and arrive at a mission cockpit. There they can play through a full year and see the Sun skim the horizon, long shadows sweep the terrain, and Earth rise and set behind the mountains. Every number on screen comes from our own calculations.

How does it work?

Near the south pole the Sun stays within one or two degrees of the horizon, and Earth moves up and down along it. Whether a site is lit or in contact with Earth therefore depends on the real terrain horizon. Our Python core calculates a 360-degree horizon profile for each site at 0.1-degree steps. It uses NASA LOLA elevation maps at 20 m resolution for nearby terrain and 80 m resolution for mountains up to 300 km away, and it accounts for the Moon’s curvature exactly. It computes hourly positions of the Sun and Earth with NASA/JPL SPICE (DE421) for 2026 to 2030 and treats the Sun as a disk rather than a point. The web interface turns these results into a live 3D scene: real-scale terrain, the Sun and a phase-correct Earth in their true directions, a lander with a communication beam, and an “astronaut eye” view from 2 m above the ground. A sky radar shows the Sun and Earth against the terrain horizon, and an event feed lists every sunrise, long night, and communication loss.

What benefits does it have?

It shows why the real horizon matters. One button switches to a flat-horizon assumption: at Malapert Massif, a flat horizon gives 50.0% sunlight and a longest night of 17.7 days, while the real terrain gives 65.4% and 14.3 days. Users can test scenarios that are recalculated in the browser. One is the antenna mask: at Mons Mouton Plateau, Earth is visible 99.4% of the time with a 0-degree mask but 81.1% with a 1-degree mask. Another is a battery simulation that shows whether a mission survives the long nights, the smallest battery that lasts the year, and the safe landing window (with example values, not real vehicle data). A simple mode shows three large numbers and one sentence for teachers and the public.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want to give mission planners a tool that shows power and Earth communication together for any site and date within seconds. We also want to make lunar polar illumination easy for anyone to understand. NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS 5228) shows this scene as a single pre-rendered video; we generate it live for every region and every date. Our results are preliminary, and we are validating them against NASA’s illumination maps.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We wrote the calculation core in Python and checked it with 30 pytest tests. We cross-checked the Sun and Earth positions with the Skyfield library; the two agree within 0.02 degrees. The interface uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with three.js for the 3D scene and the HTML Canvas for the map, sky radar, timeline, and 2D panorama. Our data sources are NASA LRO/LOLA elevation maps (Barker et al. 2023, PGDA product 90), USGS Artemis III region polygons (McClernan 2024), and NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels. We used Claude (Anthropic), an SI assistant, to help design and code the interface prototype; all scientific numbers come from our own calculation core. We needed no special hardware: we developed on our personal computers, and the app runs in a standard web browser. If WebGL is unavailable, it falls back to a 2D view in which all the numbers still work.
